title: Climate Change Education Found Lacking
main_content:
How climate change is being taught to American middle- and high-school students is severely lacking, according to a recent nationwide survey.

The National Center for Science Education (NCSE), along with the Penn State University Survey Research Center, interviewed more than 1,500 teachers and found that “three out of five teachers were unaware of, or actively misinformed about, the near total scientific consensus on climate change.”

The survey also found that teachers who want to teach climate change have a hard time accessing available information. “There are some great climate education resources out there,” said NCSE’s climate maven Minda Berbeco. “But many teachers don’t have time to find and evaluate these materials.”

Those who are more skeptical of climate change did not think the survey was sophisticated enough to account for the nuances of climate change.

“The Penn State survey of earth science teachers simplistically labels teachers who do not teach an alarmist view as deniers,” said Patrick Michaels, director of the Center for the Study of Science at the Cato Institute, who has been called a skeptic.

“A more sophisticated survey would have recognized that there is a broad spectrum of warming in the scientific literature, from modest and possibly beneficial to large and disastrous,” he said. “It is also true that there is no science behind the notion that there will be no detectable change in climate from increasing carbon dioxide, which is a true denier position.”

questions.question: What did the survey reveal?
options: The majority of teachers fully support the teaching of climate change.
Three out of five teachers were unaware or misinformed about scientific consensus on climate change.
Most teachers feel that climate change is not important enough to include in their curriculum.
Teachers believe climate change resources are too advanced for middle- and high-school students.
questions.answer: Three out of five teachers were unaware or misinformed about scientific consensus on climate change.

questions.question: Is information on climate change readily available to teachers?
options: Yes, all teachers have easy access to high-quality climate education resources.
No, many teachers struggle to find and evaluate available information.
Resources are widely available, but teachers choose not to use them.
Only urban teachers have access to climate change educational resources.
questions.answer: No, many teachers struggle to find and evaluate available information.

questions.question: What are skeptics saying about the survey?
options: They believe the survey accurately reflects the views of all teachers.
They argue that the survey overlooks the complexity of scientific opinions on climate change.
They support the survey's findings and demand more urgent climate education.
They claim the survey is biased toward alarmist views of climate change.
questions.answer: They argue that the survey overlooks the complexity of scientific opinions on climate change.
